Assessment preparation gets harder when the evidence exists but nobody can find it.

A configuration export, ticket, policy, log sample, or test record is useful only when the team can retrieve the correct version and explain what it demonstrates. A folder full of files without owners, dates, scope, or context creates more questions during review.

At Cloud2e, CMMC preparation includes evidence logistics: organizing artifacts by control, scheduling the people who can explain the work, preparing demonstration environments, and assigning one owner for the assessment relationship. The intended benefit is a clearer, more coordinated review process—not a promise about the outcome.

Start with one control family. Build an index showing the artifact name, storage location, owner, collection date, covered environment, and the question it helps answer. Then ask someone who did not create the record to retrieve it and explain the connection.

If that handoff is difficult, improve the index before adding more files.

Evidence readiness is a logistics discipline before it becomes an assessment-week activity.

Teams may have policies, configuration exports, tickets, diagrams, training records, and test results. The challenge is presenting the correct artifact, for the correct environment, with an owner who can explain how it connects to the implemented practice.

Cloud2e's assessment-preparation approach emphasizes staging artifacts by control, calendaring the right participants, preparing demonstration environments, and assigning one person to coordinate the assessor relationship. This helps turn a collection of files into an organized review process without promising a certification result.

Build an evidence-readiness packet with:
- artifact name and storage location
- control or practice connection
- system, enclave, or business process covered
- owner and backup contact
- collection and review dates
- explanation of what the artifact demonstrates
- planned interview or demonstration support

Test retrieval before the formal review. Give a colleague one evidence request and see whether the correct record and context can be produced without relying on the original author.
